conventions.convention: The Fourier transform has phase exp(−2πi x·ξ). The detector ramp multiplier is 2π|σ|, and the inverse-potential multiplier is (2π|ξ|)⁻¹, assigned value zero at ξ=0.
θ is the unit line normal, θ⊥=(−θ₂,θ₁), and the line coordinates are x=sθ+tθ⊥. Full data include all oriented normals; (θ,s) and (−θ,−s) represent the same unoriented line.
Backprojection integrates over the full polar surface measure μ(E)=2λ₂({rθ: θ∈E, 0<r≤1}); the inversion scale is 1/(4π). The normal-operator theorem assumes Countable Choice.
The continuous procedure accepts exact full sinograms of compactly supported smooth complex functions. It supplies no finite-sampling, truncation, or noise guarantee.

The finite example uses eight full-circle directions, detector bins s_m=m−2, the unnormalised negative-sign DFT with inverse factor 1/4, sampled ramp λ_k=2π min(k,4−k)/4, and angular weight π/4. Its array is synthetic.

load_bearing.statement: For f∈C_c^∞(R²;C), Rf(θ,s)=∫_R f(sθ+tθ⊥)dt, with θ⊥=(−θ₂,θ₁), compact-support Riemann integration, and Fourier phase exp(−2πi x·ξ).
For every f∈C_c^∞(R²;C), every θ∈S¹, and every σ∈R, the offset Fourier transform satisfies Fourier(Rf)(θ,σ)=Fourier(f)(σθ).
Assume Countable Choice and use the stated full polar surface measure. For every f∈C_c^∞(R²;C) and every x∈R², R*Rf(x)=4π|D|⁻¹f(x) and f(x)=(1/(4π))R*|D_s|Rf(x).

Assume Countable Choice. Given the exact full sinogram g=Rf of some f∈C_c^∞(R²;C), Fourier transform each detector row, multiply by 2π|σ|, inverse transform, backproject over the full polar surface measure, and divide by 4π.

seams_checked.note: The line-normal definition and compact-support slice citations preserve the domain, phase, and all real frequencies. General Schwartz inputs use a separately defined extension and separate slice lemma. The distinction between choice-free compact-support Riemann arguments and Countable Choice for Lebesgue identification is explicit. Batch 36 has no reverse citation to this page.

This is a page prerequisite. The geodesic definition independently specifies unit-speed integration to first exit; it does not invoke the Euclidean Fourier-slice or inversion theorem on curved surfaces. No direct item citation or reverse citation misstates a batch-36 result.

The Euclidean examples preserve s=x·θ and θ⊥=(−θ₂,θ₁). Their incidence calculation gives ξ=τθ and angular data component −τ x·θ⊥, consistently with those conventions.
